requirements.status_reason: No: the LED NIR kidney study cannot be quoted as proof of readiness, and guiding tumour-boundary decisions on patients needs validation beyond a first assessment.
requirements.answer: The LED NIR kidney study is an in vitro proof of concept on 14 samples from 7 patients, with very high variance and unacceptable false negatives, so it cannot be quoted as proof that a sensor is ready for surgical boundary decisions. A first laboratory step is to test a combined mid-IR ATR and fluorescence probe on histology-referenced tissue pairs, with the best single method as comparison. Surgical use would need validation beyond this assessment.

inline.headline: Test MIR ATR + Fluorescence combined probe on histology-referenced tissue pairs in the lab before any surgical use
inline.probe: combined ZrO2 ATR head with fluorescence, analysing the same spot (about 2 mm IR and 1 mm fluorescence areas)
inline.install: laboratory bench on ex vivo tissue surface; no surgical install assessed
inline.fiber: PIR polycrystalline fiber (3-16 µm) for MIR ATR, plus silica Vis-NIR fiber (350-2400 nm) for fluorescence
inline.test_against: best single method (fiber NIR probe) on the same validation data
inline.not_final_because: Only a laboratory concept: the combined probe was shown on model biological tissue and the fused approach is limited to fluorescent, ATR-suitable samples; no in vivo or kidney data with a fused probe exists.

problems.text: The kidney study does not prove surgical readiness: it tested two prototypes on 14 in vitro samples from 7 patients, and the authors call it a proof of concept with very high variance and unacceptable false negatives.

The study can only be quoted as an in vitro proof of concept that the LED NIR sensor captured tumour-related variance in kidney samples; the surgical scenario is an application concept with no validation data.
The kidney samples were thawed frozen biopsies measured ex vivo, and their spectra can differ from real in vivo measurements during surgery.

Without new in vivo data or validation on your own setup, the result cannot be transferred to a different sensor, organ or probe; the study used only four NIR LEDs and says the LED set must be adapted to each tissue type.

methods.why: A combined fiber probe for MIR ATR and fluorescence was shown to detect tumour boundary in the cited work and to separate tissue classes that neither method separated alone, but only for fluorescent, ATR-suitable samples.
NIR penetrates about 3 mm in tissue and is the most common online fiber-probe method, and it is the single-method comparison for the fused test; no fiber-based NIR data exist for kidney cancer.
Raman is complementary to mid-IR but needs special probes, gives weak signals and can be masked by fluorescence, so it is only worth adding if the first pair fails.

questions.q: Which organ and tissue exactly will be measured, and what must the boundary decision separate (tumour from normal tissue, which margin)?
questions.why: The LED set and the fused method must be chosen per tissue type.

questions.q: Will the probe measure in vivo during surgery, and how will it reach the tissue surface?
questions.why: Frozen or thawed ex vivo spectra can differ from in vivo spectra, and access route defines the probe.

questions.q: Can you supply histology-referenced tissue pairs from an independent laboratory as the reference?
questions.why: Histological labels are the independent reference against which any classification must be validated.

questions.q: What maximum false-negative rate and accuracy would be acceptable as the go/no-go limit?
questions.why: False negatives are unacceptable in oncology, so the limit defines the test pass criteria.

questions.q: Do the target tissues contain a fluorescent component and are they suitable for ATR contact?
questions.why: The fused approach is limited to samples with at least one fluorescent component and suitable for ATR.

experiment.objective: Test whether a combined MIR ATR and fluorescence probe separates histology-defined tumour from normal tissue better than the best single method on the same validation data.
steps: Collect paired tumour and normal tissue samples with histology from an independent laboratory as reference.
Measure each sample with the combined ZrO2 ATR head at the same spot, using five points per sample as in the cited design.
Record fiber NIR spectra from the same spots as the single-method comparison.
Build PCA or PLS-DA models per method and one low-level fused model; validate with segmented cross-validation and randomisation tests.
Check the key bands (amide 1640 and 1548 cm-1, ester 1740 cm-1, fluorescence 613 nm and 520-530 nm) and review the false negatives.
references: S04 combined MIR-ATR and fluorescence probe study
S03 LED NIR kidney feasibility study
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client: the fused model must beat the best single method on the same validation data and meet the client's false-negative limit.

pathway.key_features: Ester carbonyl near 1740 cm-1 and amide I/II near 1640 and 1548 cm-1 in the IR spectra; fluorescence bands at 613 nm (porphyrin) and 520-530 nm (FAD).
pathway.path_reason: The AFS pathway starts with a multi-method laboratory test on the customer's samples before any customised solution is chosen.

multispectral.why: Mid-IR detects the ester and amide bands of tissue while fluorescence detects FAD and porphyrin emission, so the two carry complementary information.
multispectral.test: Show that the fused model beats the best single method (IR-only or fluorescence-only, plus the NIR comparison) on the same segmented cross-validation data with histology reference.

assumptions: The proposed sensor is the LED NIR prototype family described in the kidney study.
The use case is an intraoperative tumour-boundary decision on patients.
The tissue is kidney or a related soft tissue, not stated by the client.
No validation data beyond the cited studies exist for the client's setup.
